transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in today?

Well, honestly, Dr. [Name], I'm here because... I just don't know what else to do at this point. For the last couple of years, I've just felt so low all the time. It's like this constant, heavy, empty feeling that just never really lifts, you know? And it doesn't matter what I'm doing or who I'm with. I could be at work—I inspect and weigh materials at this factory, which is tedious enough, but even when I'm just sorting things and trying to focus, that heaviness is right there with me. Or even when I'm at church, surrounded by my congregation and people I genuinely care about, people who care about me, I still feel so hollow inside. I used to think it was just a phase, like maybe I was just stressed from taking some college classes on top of working, but the classes ended and the feeling stayed. It's just always there, this dark cloud that won't go away, and I'm just so exhausted from carrying it around every single day for years now.
Have you noticed that you don't enjoy things as much as you used to, or that you've lost interest in activities you once found pleasurable?

Well... I don't think so. I mean, I wouldn't say I've lost interest in things. I honestly haven't really noticed anything like that. I still do all the same things I've always done, and I feel like I still care about them just as much. 

Like, I was mentioning church earlier—I still go every single Sunday, and I still help out with the youth group, like when we do the summer car washes or the holiday bake sales. I still really want to be there for all of that. I haven't lost any interest in it at all. And I still like hanging out with my friends from when I was taking those college classes. We try to get together at least once a month, usually at this little diner right down the street from the factory where I do my inspecting. I still look forward to it all week, you know? I still like going there, ordering my usual, and catching up on all their drama. 

So it's not that I don't find those things pleasurable anymore, because I do, I really do. It's more just... that dark cloud I was talking about is just sitting on my shoulders the whole time I'm doing them. But the interest is definitely still there. I haven't stopped liking my hobbies either. I still read a ton, mostly fantasy novels, which I've been completely obsessed with since I was in middle school, and I still go out of my way to buy the new releases the exact day they come out. 

So, no, I definitely wouldn't say I've lost interest or stopped enjoying things. I'm just... doing the things I enjoy while feeling completely weighed down by this sadness, if that makes any sense? Because I really do still like all my regular activities, I just can't seem to shake the heavy feeling while I'm participating in them.
Do you find that you feel fatigued or lacking in energy most days, even if you’ve had enough rest?

Oh, definitely. Honestly, that's one of the hardest parts of all of this. It's just... yes, I am so tired all the time. And it's incredibly frustrating because I really do try to get enough rest, you know? Like, on my days off from the factory, I'll sometimes sleep for ten or eleven hours, or I'll just spend the whole day on the couch doing absolutely nothing, thinking that if I just let my body rest, I'll finally wake up feeling recharged. But resting on my days off doesn't really refill me at all. I wake up feeling just as drained as when I went to sleep, like my battery is permanently stuck at one percent. 

And because of that, even the really small stuff feels like it takes way more energy than I actually have. Like at work, after I finish checking a batch of materials, I have to fill out these daily inspection logs. It’s literally just writing down a few numbers, checking some boxes, and signing my name, but sometimes I just stare at the clipboard because lifting the pen feels like a monumental task. My arms just feel so heavy. 

And it’s the same with my personal life. Like, driving to basketball—I still want to go, but just the physical act of grabbing my keys, walking out to the car, and navigating the traffic just wipes me out completely. By the time I get there, I'm already spent. Or even something as basic as washing my hair! You wouldn't think taking a shower would be exhausting, but just standing there and holding my arms up to scrub the shampoo in... half the time I just want to sit down on the floor of the tub because it's too much effort to keep my hands raised. I just never have any energy for anything, no matter how much I sleep or how easy the task is supposed to be. It's like I'm moving through wet cement from the minute I wake up until I go back to sleep.
Have you found yourself feeling worthless or guilty about things, even when there’s no real reason to feel that way?

Worthless? Or guilty? Um... no, actually, I don't really get that at all. I mean, I know I'm not worthless. Even with this huge, heavy cloud hanging over me all the time, I still know I have value, you know? Like, at the factory, my job is actually really important, even if it is super repetitive. If I don't weigh and inspect those materials exactly right, or if I let a bad batch through, the whole production line gets messed up later on. So I know I'm contributing something useful there, I know they need me to do it right. And at church, the kids in the youth group—they really look up to me. I know I matter to them, and I know I matter to my friends from my old college classes, too. So I definitely don't feel worthless. 

And as for feeling guilty... I don't really have that either. I mean, sure, sometimes I feel a little bummed if I'm just too exhausted to stay out late at the diner with my friends, but it's not like this deep, agonizing guilt where I'm beating myself up over things that aren't my fault. I know I'm doing the absolute best I can with how completely drained and sad I feel. I don't sit around thinking I'm a burden to people or that I've done something wrong to deserve this. 

It's actually kind of weird, I guess, because you always hear about people who are sad and they just hate themselves, but I really don't hate myself. I just hate this feeling. Like, just the other day, my mom called and she was asking if I was okay because I guess I sounded really flat on the phone, and I didn't feel guilty for worrying her, I just felt... frustrated, I guess, that I couldn't sound more upbeat for her. I know she loves me, and I know my worth as a daughter and a friend and a worker. So, yeah, no guilt really, and definitely no feelings of being worthless. I know who I am, I just... I just wish who I am wasn't carrying around this invisible lead blanket all day. But I definitely don't blame myself for it, if that makes sense.
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to think clearly, concentrate, or make decisions lately?

Um... no, I wouldn't say that. My thinking is actually pretty clear, honestly. I haven't noticed any brain fog or anything like that. 

Like, I was just mentioning my job at the factory, and even though it's really repetitive, it actually requires a ton of focus. I'm an inspector and weigher, right? So I'm constantly looking at these tiny little variations in the materials, and I have to read the digital scales, which go down to, like, the hundredth of an ounce. If my concentration was slipping, I would definitely be making mistakes. But my accuracy rate is still exactly where it's always been. I know this because my supervisor, Brenda, posts these weekly quality control charts on the bulletin board in the break room—which, honestly, is a whole other thing because nobody actually likes that she does that, it feels a bit like public shaming for the people who mess up—but anyway, my name is always right at the top for zero defects. I can stand there for my whole shift and focus perfectly on the numbers and the quality checks. So I'm definitely still able to concentrate on the fine details, even when my body feels completely exhausted.

And as for making decisions... no, that hasn't changed either. I mean, I don't have to make huge, life-altering decisions every single day, but even for the normal stuff, I don't find myself getting stuck or second-guessing myself. Like when we were planning the youth group car wash last month, the pastor asked me to figure out the volunteer schedule and decide who was going to be on the washing station versus the drying station. I just looked at the list of kids, knew immediately who would goof off too much with the hoses, and made the assignments in like five minutes. No hesitation at all. 

Plus, like I said, I read those huge fantasy novels. You know the ones—they're like eight hundred pages long with massive maps in the front and glossaries in the back because there are just so many characters and different kingdoms to keep track of. I can still sit down and read a hundred pages in one sitting without my mind wandering off. I don't have to go back and re-read paragraphs because I forgot what just happened or because I zoned out. I'm right there in the story, keeping all the plotlines straight. 

So, yeah, my brain works fine, my concentration is totally normal, and I can decide things just as quickly as I always could. It's really just that heavy, sad feeling and the total lack of physical energy that I'm dealing with. My actual brain power hasn't taken a hit at all. Because honestly, if I couldn't focus, I'd probably get fired by Brenda, and thankfully I'm still doing my job perfectly fine.
Have you ever had a period of time where you felt unusually high, overly energetic, or irritable, where you didn’t feel like you needed as much sleep or where you were more impulsive than usual?

Unusually high or energetic? Oh, wow, no. I mean... I honestly can't even imagine what that would feel like at this point. Like I was saying before about the wet cement feeling? It's just always that. Always heavy. I've never had a time where I was bouncing off the walls or feeling like I could take on the world or anything like that. Honestly, I kind of wish I could borrow some of that energy you're talking about, just to get through a normal shift without feeling like my arms are going to fall off. But no, never. 

And the sleep thing... definitely not. I mean, I love sleep. I *need* sleep. Like I said, I'll sleep ten or eleven hours if I can. I can't even fathom waking up after, like, three or four hours and feeling ready to go. That sounds like a literal superpower to me, because I'm the exact opposite. Even back when I was taking my college classes, before I took a break to work at the factory full-time, I was never one of those people pulling all-nighters and feeling fine the next day. I always, always needed my rest, and lately I need it more than ever, even if it doesn't actually refresh me. 

As for being impulsive or, you know, doing things without thinking... that's really not me at all. I'm a super cautious person. I think things through probably way more than I need to. Like, even if I'm just deciding what to get at the diner with my friends, I'll sit there reading the menu for ten minutes weighing my options, even though I almost always just get the exact same turkey club sandwich anyway. I just don't jump into things blindly. 

And at work, being an inspector, you literally can't be impulsive. You have to follow the standard operating procedure step by step by step, every single time. If I just started doing things on a whim or making snap decisions without checking the scales, I'd ruin the whole batch of materials and Brenda would definitely have my head. So, yeah, I've never had a phase like that where I'm just reckless or overly hyper or irritable. I'm usually pretty even-keeled, just... really, really drained. It's always just been this constant, exhausting low, never a high.
Have you noticed that your movements or speech have slowed down, or that you feel restless or fidgety, more than usual?

Um... no, I wouldn't say that. I know I keep talking about how heavy I feel, like that wet cement feeling, but that's more of an internal exhaustion, you know? It doesn't actually make my body move in slow motion or make me talk super slow. 

Like, if you watched me at work, you wouldn't think I was moving any slower than anyone else. The conveyor belt at the factory doesn't wait for anybody, so if my hands were actually moving sluggishly, the samples would just pile up at my station, and I'd totally miss my quota. I have to pull the material, get it on the digital scale, log the exact weight, and push it back down the line in, like, seconds. If I was physically slowed down, Brenda—my supervisor—she would be right there behind me with her clipboard, tapping her pen and asking why I'm holding up the entire production floor. But I keep up just fine. My hands do exactly what they need to do at the normal speed. And my speech is normal, too. I mean, I mentioned earlier that my mom said I sounded flat on the phone the other day, but she didn't say I was talking slow. I still talk at the exact same pace I always have, whether I'm explaining a game to the youth group kids or just ordering my turkey club at the diner. 

And as for being restless or fidgety... oh gosh, no. I honestly don't even have the energy to fidget. When I sit down, I just sit. I don't bounce my leg, I don't pace the room, I don't tap my fingers. My friend Sarah, whenever we go out, she's constantly shaking her knee or peeling the paper labels off her water bottle, and honestly, just watching her do all that nervous movement makes me feel even more tired. When I get a chance to sit down, whether it's in the break room or on my couch at home, I am completely still. I just want to rest my body because of how incredibly drained I am. 

So I definitely don't have this urge to pace around or move constantly. It's almost the exact opposite of restless, really. I just want to lay flat and not move a single muscle, but when I *do* have to move and do my job, I move at a totally normal speed. So, yeah, no slow-motion talking and definitely no pacing or fidgeting.
How long has this feeling of sadness or heaviness been present? Has it been going on for more than two years?

Um, yeah... it's definitely been more than two years. Actually, I know exactly how long it’s been, because it started right around a very specific turning point for me. It’s been about two years and four months, to be exact. 

I know that sounds oddly specific, but that was when I had to stop taking my classes at the community college. I was trying to get my basics out of the way, you know? I really liked my classes, especially this one psychology elective I was in, but... well, the money just wasn't there. Between the tuition going up and just trying to afford gas and basic things, I was getting so stressed out. And then my work schedule at the factory just got completely unmanageable with school. Brenda—my supervisor, the one with the clipboard I mentioned earlier—she needed me to cover these longer shifts because we were short-staffed on the inspection line, and I just couldn't balance the hours on the production floor with the time I needed to actually be in a classroom and studying. 

So, I had to make the call to drop out. And it was right then, two years and four months ago, that this whole... this heavy, exhausting cloud just kind of descended on me. I remember going to the registrar's office to fill out the official withdrawal paperwork, and it was just this awful, sinking feeling in my chest. And honestly, that feeling just never went away. I told myself at the time, like, I'll just take a semester off, save up some money from the extra factory shifts, and go back in the spring. But the months just kept passing, and the money never seemed to stretch far enough, and the whole time—every single day for over two years now—I've just felt that same heavy, drained sadness. 

It's like my life just paused that day in the registrar's office, you know? I just go to the factory, do my weighing and inspecting, come home, sleep for ten hours, and do it all over again. I haven't been back to the campus since. So, yeah, it hasn't just been a few weeks or months of feeling like this. It’s been a really, really long time. Two years and four months of just... wading through wet cement.

Looking back over the past two years, have you ever noticed any days or periods when your body felt physically slowed down, like your movements were sluggish, or when you felt unusually restless or unable to sit still, even if just for a short time?

Um, well, I know you're asking about that whole two-year timeframe now, since I just told you exactly how long this has been going on, but... honestly, my answer is pretty much the exact same as what I was just saying a minute ago. Even looking back over the entire two years and four months since I had to leave my classes, I really haven't had any days where my body physically slowed down or where I got restless. 

I mean, if I had ever actually started moving sluggishly, I would definitely remember it, because it would have been a massive issue at work. Like I was explaining with the factory line, I just can't afford to be physically slow. Every single day for those two years, I've clocked in, put on my heavy steel-toed boots, stood at my inspection station, and kept up with the conveyor belt. There was actually this one time, maybe a year or so ago, where we had this massive, unexpected influx of materials to sort and weigh because another plant went offline, and I remember being so mentally and emotionally exhausted that I honestly thought I was going to just start crying right there on the production floor. But my hands? My hands were still moving at the exact same speed they always do. Pulling the samples, checking the digital readout, logging the numbers on the clipboard, pushing it down the line. It's just pure muscle memory at this point. My brain feels like it's wading through that wet cement I keep talking about, but my physical body just keeps doing the motions at a totally normal pace. 

And as for feeling restless or not being able to sit still over these past couple of years... no, definitely not. If anything, the longer this whole thing goes on, the more completely still I am whenever I'm actually allowed to stop moving. When I get home to my apartment after a long shift, I take off those heavy boots and I just sit on the couch. I don't pace the hallway, I don't tap my feet, I don't get up to reorganize things. Sometimes I'll literally just sit there for an hour in my work clothes before I even remember to turn on the TV or get a glass of water, just staring at the wall because I'm so completely drained. 

My friend Sarah, the one I mentioned who's always peeling the labels off her water bottles and bouncing her knee? She's always telling me I need to get up and go for a walk or do some yoga or something active to, like, "shake off the funk," as she calls it. But I just don't have that urge in my body at all. I don't have any restless energy to burn off. My body just wants to sink into the couch cushions and stay there forever. So, yeah, looking back over the whole two years since I dropped out... not a single day of moving in slow motion, and definitely not a single day of being restless. Just that same constant, heavy exhaustion.

Before this current period of sadness that started two years and four months ago, did you ever have a time when you felt down or depressed for a period of time, even if it was shorter or less intense than what you're feeling now?

Um, before that? Before the whole dropping out thing two years and four months ago? No... no, definitely not. Honestly, that’s part of why this whole thing has been so incredibly hard to deal with, because before I had to leave school, I was actually... well, I was fine. I was doing really great, actually. 

Like, in high school, I was just your totally normal teenager. I mean, sure, I’d get stressed out about finals or drama with friends or whatever, but I never had anything even close to this heavy, dark feeling. And then when I graduated and started at the factory to pay for my community college classes, I was actually super energized about my life. I had this whole plan, you know? I’d work my shifts on the inspection line, make my money, go to my classes, and I still had energy left over to actually go out and do things. I used to go get coffee with Sarah almost every weekend, and we’d talk for hours about what we were going to do with our lives. I was taking that psychology elective I told you about, and an English comp class, and I was just really excited about the future. 

So, no, I never had any periods of feeling down or depressed before all this. If I had a bad day back then, it was just a bad day. I’d sleep it off and wake up feeling totally fine the next morning. It really wasn’t until that exact time, when the tuition got too high and Brenda started scheduling me for all those extra mandatory shifts and I realized I literally couldn't do both... that was when the bottom just completely fell out. It really felt like a light switch flipped the day I signed those withdrawal papers. Before that day, I was completely normal. I didn't have any of this exhaustion or this constant sadness. It just... it all started right then, and it just hasn't stopped since. So, yeah, looking back before that two-year-and-four-month mark, there was absolutely nothing like this. It was just a totally normal life.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight since this sadness started—like eating a lot more or a lot less than usual, or gaining or losing weight without trying?

Um, yeah, actually... food has just become this huge chore since all this started. It’s really weird because I used to actually care about what I ate, but now... most days, I just don't have an appetite at all. Nothing ever sounds good. I'll wake up and the thought of making breakfast or packing a lunch is just exhausting, so I just don't. I'll literally skip eating for almost the entire day. I'll clock in, go stand at my inspection station, and I won't eat anything until my shift is almost completely over. Sometimes Brenda will practically force me to go take my scheduled break, and I'll just sit there in the breakroom staring at the table because the idea of chewing just feels like too much work. 

But then, what happens is I get so unbelievably drained from standing there on the line for eight or ten hours on nothing but fumes, that I just kind of hit a wall. And when that happens, usually really late in the shift or right before I drag myself home, I end up just standing in front of the vending machines in the breakroom. I'll just grab whatever junk is in there—chips, candy bars, those little powdered donuts—just because I'm so physically and mentally drained and I know I won't have the energy to actually cook a real meal when I get back to my apartment. 

And because I'm either starving myself all day because nothing sounds good, or just surviving on vending machine snacks late at night, my weight has just been completely all over the place. It’s been up and down so much over these past couple of years without me even trying to do anything to it. Like, I have these thick, heavy-duty work pants that I have to wear on the production floor, right? And I swear, they fit completely different from month to month. One month I'm having to pull my belt as tight as it can possibly go because the pants are practically falling off me from skipping meals, and then the next month the waistband is digging into my stomach because I've been living off breakroom junk food for weeks. It’s just this constant, exhausting back and forth, and it just makes putting on my uniform every morning that much more depressing because I never know how my clothes are going to feel.
Have you had a depressed mood most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years?

Um, yeah. Honestly, that’s exactly why I’m here. Because for the last couple of years—pretty much exactly since that two-year-and-four-month mark when I had to drop my classes—I just feel low all the time. And I mean *all* the time. It’s not just a bad afternoon here or there, it’s most of the day, every single day. 

It’s just this... this heavy, empty feeling that doesn’t really lift, no matter what I’m doing or where I am. Like, I could be at work, standing right there on the factory line doing my inspections, and it’s just weighing me down. Or even if I'm somewhere else, like at church, you know, where you're supposed to feel, I don't know, peaceful or uplifted or connected to something? I just sit there in the pew and feel completely hollow. 

And it's even like that when I’m around people I really care about, which is probably the hardest part. Like with my friend Sarah, when she actually manages to drag me out of my apartment to get coffee like we used to before all this started. I’ll be sitting right across the little café table from her, and she’s talking and trying to cheer me up or tell me about her week, and I just can't connect to it at all. The heavy feeling is just always there, right in the middle of everything. 

It’s like I’m carrying around this massive, invisible weight in my chest from the second I wake up and put my work boots on, to the second I finally go back to sleep. It never takes a day off. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday on the production floor or a Sunday morning... it just never, ever lifts. So, yeah, to answer your question, definitely more days than not. Honestly, it's been every single day for the last couple of years.
Looking back at your time at work, church, or with friends, have you noticed any days when you truly didn’t care about being there or felt no pleasure at all, even in things you used to enjoy?

Um, I don't... I don't think so? Like, it’s not that I don’t care about being there. I actually care a lot. Maybe even too much, you know? It’s just... it’s different from not caring. Like with Sarah, when we go to the café, I still really want to see her. I still love her, and I still want to hear all about her week and what she's doing in her classes, because I still care about her just as much as I always did. It’s not like I sit there thinking, "I don't want to be here" or "I don't care about my best friend anymore." I definitely do. I still enjoy her company. It's just that I feel so incredibly heavy and sad while I'm doing it. The caring is completely still there, I promise, it’s just buried under all that heaviness I was telling you about.

And even with work... I mean, obviously, nobody is jumping for joy to stand at an inspection station for ten hours a day, looking at the exact same parts over and over. But I still care about doing my job right. I don't just zone out and let defective pieces slide by because I don't care. I still feel that sense of responsibility, and I still want to do a good job so Brenda doesn't yell at me. I haven't lost my work ethic or my drive to do things correctly. 

And church, too. I still really want to go every Sunday. I still think the music is beautiful, and I still want to listen to the choir, and I still value being part of that community. I haven't lost my interest in my faith or anything like that. I just sit there and feel that horrible hollow sadness instead of feeling uplifted like I used to. So, no, I wouldn't say I've lost interest or stopped caring about things, or that I don't get any pleasure out of them at all. It's more like... the things I love are still the things I love, but I just have to experience them through this awful, thick filter of sadness now. Does that make sense? Because I really don't want you to think I've just given up on caring about my life or the people in it. I really haven't. It's just the sadness that's the problem.

In the past two years, have you ever experienced periods lasting several days or more when you felt down or lost interest in things, along with other symptoms such as changes in sleep, appetite, or feelings of worthlessness?

Um... I'm a little confused by how you're wording that, I guess? Because when you say periods lasting several days or more, that makes it sound like... like it's something that comes and goes, you know? Like I might have three or four bad days where I'm feeling down, and then I snap out of it and have a good week, and then maybe I have another bad few days later on. 

But it's really not like that at all for me. Like I was saying before, it doesn't take a break. It's not a specific period of time, it's just my whole life now. It's literally every single day. I wake up, put on my work boots, go to the plant, stand at my inspection station, come home, and that heavy sadness is just sitting right there on my chest the entire time. There aren't any breaks where I feel normal, so there aren't really periods of feeling down—it's just a constant, endless flatline. 

And as for the other stuff you just mentioned, like losing interest or feeling worthless... no, I really don't think I have that. I know I just talked a lot about the interest thing, but I really want to make sure I'm explaining it right so you understand, because I still care so much about Sarah, and my church, and even doing my job right. I don't just lose interest in my life for a few days and then magically get it back. 

And I definitely don't feel worthless, either. I mean, I know I'm a hard worker. Brenda, my supervisor, she knows she can count on me to catch the defects on the line. She trusts me to do the quality checks because she knows I won't let bad parts slip through, and I know I'm a good friend to Sarah, even if I'm not exactly the life of the party right now. I don't sit around my apartment thinking I'm a worthless person or that I don't have value or anything like that. I just feel incredibly, overwhelmingly sad all the time. So, no, I wouldn't say I have these specific patches of days where things suddenly change and I lose interest or feel worthless... it's just that exact same, steady heaviness I've had every single day since I dropped my classes.
Looking back at your life before this sadness started, have you noticed that you no longer enjoy things that used to give you pleasure, even if you still participate in them?

Um, wait, isn't that... isn't that kind of what you just asked me? I mean, I'm sorry, I don't want to sound rude or anything, I just feel like I'm maybe not explaining myself right if we're still on this. Because I really haven't lost the enjoyment of things. It's not like everything I used to love has just gone totally numb or turned grey or something. 

Like, if Sarah and I go to that little café—the one over on 4th street where we always get those iced vanilla lattes, even in the middle of winter, which is just this silly tradition we started back when I was still in classes before I had to drop out—I still genuinely enjoy the taste of the coffee. And I still genuinely enjoy hearing her laugh when she tells me about her week. It still brings me a feeling of, you know, pleasure, just like it always did. The enjoyment itself hasn't gone anywhere at all. It's just that I'm also carrying this massive boulder of sadness at the exact same time. 

It's like... okay, imagine you're eating your absolute favorite meal in the whole world, something you really, really enjoy, but you have a terrible, pounding headache while you're eating it. You still like the food, right? You still enjoy the taste, you haven't lost your ability to like your favorite meal, but the headache is just making the whole experience really heavy and exhausting to get through. That's exactly what it's like for me. I still enjoy my friends, I still get pleasure from hearing the choir music at church on Sunday mornings because the harmonies are just as beautiful to me now as they were three years ago, and I still like the satisfaction of catching a really tricky defect on the inspection line before Brenda even notices it. 

I haven't lost my ability to enjoy my life, I really, really haven't. I just have this constant, heavy sadness sitting right on top of all that enjoyment, every single day. So, no, I definitely wouldn't say I no longer enjoy things. I still do. I just wish I didn't have to feel so incredibly sad while I was enjoying them, you know?

In the past two years, have you ever had a period of time lasting at least two weeks where you felt worse than usual, such as feeling more hopeless, having more difficulty getting through the day, or experiencing more severe symptoms than your usual baseline?

Um, I feel like this is kind of like what you asked a minute ago about the several days thing, just... longer? Because, honestly, no. There isn't really a "worse than usual" for me, because my "usual" is already just so incredibly heavy. 

It's exactly the same every single day. I don't have these dips where suddenly for two weeks I can't get through the day, because getting through the day is exactly the same amount of difficult on a Tuesday in November as it is on a Thursday in May. It's just this constant, flat line of sadness. Like, when I'm at the plant, standing there sorting through the parts on the line, I'm not suddenly thinking, "Oh, this week is so much harder than last week, I'm struggling so much more right now." It's just the exact same slog. I clock in, I do my quality checks, Brenda assigns me my section for the shift, and I just carry that exact same heavy boulder of sadness the entire ten hours. 

I don't feel more hopeless suddenly, because the sadness is just always there at the exact same volume. It never turns up to a ten for two weeks and then goes back down to a five. It's just always, always sitting right there at a really high, heavy level, if that makes sense? Like, it doesn't fluctuate. So, no, I don't have these two-week periods where things get dramatically worse or more severe. I mean, sure, I’d get stressed out about finals or drama with friends or whatever, but I never had anything even close to this heavy, dark feeling. And then when I graduated and started at the factory to pay for my community college classes, I was actually super energized about my life. I had this whole plan, you know? I’d work my shifts on the inspection line, make my money, go to my classes, and I still had energy left over to actually go out and do things. I used to go get coffee with Sarah almost every weekend, and we’d talk for hours about what we were going to do with our lives. I was taking that psychology elective I told you about, and an English comp class, and I was just really excited about the future. 

So, no, I never had any periods of feeling down or depressed before all this. If I had a bad day back then, it was just a bad day. I’d sleep it off and wake up feeling totally fine the next morning. It really wasn’t until that exact time, when the tuition got too high and Brenda started scheduling me for all those extra mandatory shifts and I realized I literally couldn't do both... that was when the bottom just completely fell out. It really felt like a light switch flipped the day I signed those withdrawal papers. Before that day, I was completely normal. I didn't have any of this exhaustion or this constant sadness. It just... it all started right then, and it just hasn't stopped since. So, yeah, looking back before that two-year-and-four-month mark, there was absolutely nothing like this.
